parent: Distinguishing That Dhyāna's Arising Is Not Fixed

zh: 第二、明發諸禪三昧所由，自有二解不同：一、有師言：「但修上入定，諸禪自發，不勞餘習。」此師一向併用止法教人事等，舊醫純用乳藥。今不同此。所以然者，止者一法，發法亦應但一，既行者因止發禪不同，何得一向由止？此則非唯於理有失，亦是乖佛教門。二、有師言：「宿世經習諸禪，善根為因，今世修止，得定為緣，是故異發不同。」其義可見。譬如陸地雖有藥草、樹木、叢林種類若干，名色各異，若不同霑一味之雨，豈得有異類生長之殊？此亦如是，若依大乘，闇室、瓶、盆、井中七寶之義，此則別論。
en: Second, clarifying the reasons the various dhyāna-samādhis arise at all: there are, here, two differing explanations. One master says: "One need only cultivate entry into concentration as described above, and every dhyāna will arise of itself, with no need to labor over any further practice." This master relies exclusively on the method of stopping to teach students in every matter, much like an old-fashioned physician who relies solely on milk as medicine. The present treatise does not follow this view. Why is this? Stopping is a single dharma, so the dharma it brings forth ought likewise to be only one; yet since practitioners bring forth such different dhyānas through this same stopping, how could this possibly be attributed to stopping alone? Not only would this be mistaken in principle, it would also run contrary to the Buddha's own teaching-gate.

A second master says: "The various dhyānas already experienced and habituated to in past lives serve as the wholesome-root cause; cultivating stopping in this present life serves as the condition through which concentration is attained — this is why what arises differs from person to person." The meaning of this can be readily seen. It is like dry land: although it holds various kinds of medicinal herbs, trees, and thickets, each with its own name and form, if they were not all equally moistened by the same single rain, how could their different kinds possibly grow and flourish as they do? This is exactly the same. As for the sense given in the Mahāyāna teaching of the seven treasures hidden within a dark room, a vase, a basin, or a well, this is a separate discussion, treated elsewhere.

The rejected first view is a real position worth taking seriously before dismissing it: a teacher who genuinely believes one method suffices for everyone, "like an old-fashioned physician who relies solely on milk as medicine." The rain-and-vegetation simile that replaces it is the treatise's cleanest statement yet of the whole fascicle's governing logic — one uniform condition (the rain, i.e. stopping) acting on radically different latent causes (the seeds and roots already present, i.e. each practitioner's own past habituation) to produce different results. Every unpredictable-arising list in this section is really just this one image, spelled out combinatorially.

parent: Distinguishing That Dhyāna's Arising Is Not Fixed

zh: 第三、明發法多少者，上雖辨因止通發一切諸禪三昧，然行人根性不同，發法不無多少之別。有人但發一種禪門，有發二門、三門、四門、五門，或有一人並發十五門及一切諸禪三昧，不可定判。所以而然，此皆由行者過去習因偏圓不等，厚薄之殊，亦以今世精進、懈怠，有慧方便、無慧方便之別，故發法優劣不同，殊途萬品之異，是則略明發法多少之相也。
en: Third, clarifying how much dhyāna arises: although it has been distinguished above that, through stopping, every dhyāna-samādhi can be brought forth in common, practitioners' own capacities differ, and so what actually arises is not without its own difference in quantity. Some people bring forth only a single gate of dhyāna; others bring forth two gates, three, four, or five; and some single individuals bring forth all fifteen gates and every dhyāna-samādhi together — this cannot be judged as fixed in advance. Why is this so? It is entirely because practitioners' past habituation-causes are unequal in their partiality or completeness, and differ in thickness or thinness, and also because of the difference, in this present life, between diligence and laziness, and between skillful means joined with wisdom and skillful means without it — hence what arises differs in superiority and inferiority, taking countless divergent paths and forms. This, in brief, clarifies the marks of how much dhyāna arises.

Two variables compound here rather than one: how much was habituated in past lives (thick or thin, partial or complete), and how much effort and wisdom is brought to this present life's cultivation. The treatise's insistence that this "cannot be judged as fixed in advance" is consistent with everything else in this closing section — a teacher watching one student bring forth all fifteen gates while another brings forth only one has no grounds to conclude anything about either student's present diligence from that difference alone.

items.en: Whether Past Wholesome Roots Are Exhausted
parent: Distinguishing That Dhyāna's Arising Is Not Fixed

zh: 第四、明因止發禪，有盡、不盡。今就易顯者明，故先約一不淨觀中分別，自有行人宿世已經修得不淨、白骨流光。今於止中但發得不淨，未得白骨流光，此名不盡；若具足發者，名之為盡。若過去所習，勢分已盡，雖復修止，則不增進。若更專心諦觀白骨，練於骨人，研修不已即覺，隨心所觀，境界漸漸開發，成八背捨，觀、練、熏、修悉皆具足。此即是今世善巧精勤修習之所成就，非關過去習因善發。
en: Fourth, clarifying that dhyāna brought forth through stopping may or may not be fully exhausted. Here, taking what is most easily shown, this is first distinguished with reference to the contemplation of impurity alone: some practitioners have already, in past lives, cultivated and attained the contemplation of impurity together with the flowing light of the white bones. If, now, within stopping, only the contemplation of impurity is brought forth, without yet attaining the flowing light of the white bones, this is called "not exhausted"; if brought forth in full, this is called "exhausted." If what was habituated in the past has already spent its full force, then, even continuing to cultivate stopping, no further progress will be made. But if one instead applies the mind single-mindedly to contemplating the white bones in earnest, refining the skeletal figure, researching and cultivating it without pause, one will come to a realization: according to whatever the mind contemplates, the state gradually opens and develops further, coming to completion as the eight liberations, with observing, refining, perfuming, and mastering all present in full. This, however, is precisely the accomplishment of skillful, diligent cultivation in this present life, and has nothing to do with the arising of any wholesome root habituated in the past.

zh: 問曰：修止境界不進，何必由習因已盡，或由罪障障於宿善故，不得增長開發。答曰：實如來問，此別是一途，不妨自有發盡之者，非關罪障，必須方便，依如觀法修習，乃得成就。是中應歷五種根性人料揀：一、退分人；二、護分人；三、住分人；四、進分人；五、達分人。分別云云，今不具記。餘十四禪發盡、不盡相，類爾可知。
en: Question: when the state within cultivating stopping fails to progress, need this necessarily be because the habituation-cause has already been exhausted? Might it not instead be because some karmic offense is obstructing one's own past wholesome root, preventing it from growing and developing further? Answer: your question is indeed correct — this is a separate matter, a path of its own, and does not rule out that some cases are, in fact, simply exhausted, with no karmic offense involved at all; in such cases, skillful means are necessary, cultivating in reliance on the contemplative method just as described, before completion can be reached. Here, one should distinguish this by passing through five kinds of practitioner capacity: those prone to regression; those who merely maintain their ground; those who abide steadily; those who progress; and those who penetrate through. The distinctions among these are not recorded here in full. The marks of exhaustion or non-exhaustion for the remaining fourteen dhyānas may be understood by this same pattern.

The white-bones case gives this abstract "exhausted or not" distinction a concrete, almost diagnostic test: does further effort in the very same practice keep producing new depth, or has it plateaued? A plateau from an exhausted past cause calls not for a new method but for deliberate present-life effort in the same contemplation (single-mindedly contemplating the white bones and refining the skeletal figure until it develops into the eight liberations); a plateau from karmic obstruction calls for repentance instead, as established earlier in this fascicle's discussion of verifying wholesome roots. The five-fold scale of practitioner capacity (prone to regression, merely maintaining, abiding, progressing, penetrating) is a classical scheme for describing how secure an attainment is, not how deep it is — a reminder that "how far has this student gotten" and "how likely are they to keep it" are two different questions.

parent: Distinguishing That Dhyāna's Arising Is Not Fixed

zh: 第五、約有漏、無漏分別者。問曰：上明十五門諸禪三昧發相，是中自有有漏、無漏。有漏之善，過去經得，可有習因善發，無漏本未經得，豈有過去習因善發耶？答曰：無漏有二種：一者、行行無漏；二者、慧行無漏。行行無漏既是對治事法，不的據緣真，得有過去習因善發慧行無漏；既的約緣真，不可定論有過去習因善發慧行無漏。復有二種：一者、緣理修習，以明慧行；二者、發慧見理緣真，以明慧行。緣理修習，則有習因善發。發慧見理，雖復緣真，則無習因善發。
en: Fifth, distinguishing this in terms of the contaminated and the uncontaminated. Question: as clarified above, the marks of the fifteen gates of dhyāna-samādhi arising include, among them, both the contaminated and the uncontaminated. Contaminated wholesomeness, having already been experienced and attained in the past, can indeed have a habituation-cause behind its arising; but the uncontaminated was originally never experienced at all — how, then, could it possibly have a habituation-cause from the past behind its arising? Answer: the uncontaminated is of two kinds — uncontaminated conduct-practice, and uncontaminated wisdom-practice. Uncontaminated conduct-practice, being itself a phenomenal dharma serving as an antidote, does not definitely take truth itself as its object — hence it can have a habituation-cause from the past behind its arising. Uncontaminated wisdom-practice, on the other hand, does definitely take truth itself as its object — hence it cannot definitely be said to have a habituation-cause from the past behind its arising. This, too, is of two further kinds: cultivation that takes principle as its object, clarifying wisdom-practice in this sense; and the arising of wisdom that sees principle, taking truth directly as its object, clarifying wisdom-practice in this other sense. Cultivation that takes principle as its object can indeed have a habituation-cause behind its arising. The arising of wisdom that sees principle, although it, too, takes truth as its object, has no habituation-cause behind its arising.

zh: 發慧見真復有二種：一者、發相似慧；二者、發真實慧。發相似慧，或有習因善發。發真實慧，則無習因善發。發真實慧復有二種：一者、發苦忍等見諦無漏；二、發無礙解脫等三界思惟無漏。若發苦忍等見諦無漏，一向不論有習因善發。若發思惟無漏，則教門不定，若類薩婆多解意，退法，斯陀含、阿那含、阿羅漢退還初果中，後更證果，則有習因善發。若不退法，三果人既無重發之義，皆不辨有習因善發。若類曇無德解意所明，四果發真無漏，皆無習因善發。
en: The arising of wisdom that sees truth is, again, of two kinds: the arising of approximate wisdom; and the arising of true, genuine wisdom. The arising of approximate wisdom may, in some cases, have a habituation-cause behind its arising. The arising of true, genuine wisdom has no habituation-cause behind its arising. The arising of true, genuine wisdom is, again, of two kinds: the arising of uncontaminated attainment on the path of vision, such as the forbearance of suffering; and the arising of uncontaminated attainment on the path of cultivation across the three realms, such as unobstructed liberation. If uncontaminated attainment on the path of vision, such as the forbearance of suffering, arises, it is never, under any account, said to have a habituation-cause behind its arising. If uncontaminated attainment on the path of cultivation arises, the teaching on this point is not fixed: if one follows the Sarvāstivādin interpretation, then, for the retrogressible — once-returners, non-returners, and arhats who regress back to the fruit of stream-entry and later realize the fruit again — there is indeed a habituation-cause behind this arising; but for the non-retrogressible, since those who have attained the three higher fruits have, by definition, no sense of realizing them anew, none of these is distinguished as having a habituation-cause behind its arising. If one follows the interpretation given by the Dharmaguptakas, then the true, uncontaminated attainment arising at all four fruits has, in every case, no habituation-cause behind its arising.

zh: 問曰：如阿毘曇分別，但初生無漏，無有自種因，今何得一向四果所發真無漏皆無習因善發？答曰：今明諸禪三昧發習因，義意不同，是中的據過去經得之善，中間退失，今因止更發，以明習因善發。四果發真無漏，悉無先世經得、中間失退因，今修止重發，豈得為類？若通論初品心無漏真解，即為二品心無漏作，種類如是，乃至九品。約此明習因善者，則四果所發無漏，皆名習因善發也。今既不約此明習因善發，故云四果所發皆非習因善根發也。
en: Question: according to the Abhidharma's own distinction, only the very first arising of an uncontaminated state has no cause of its own kind behind it at all — how, then, can it now be said, without qualification, that the true, uncontaminated attainment arising at all four fruits has no habituation-cause behind it? Answer: what is clarified here regarding dhyāna-samādhis' arising through a habituation-cause carries a different sense altogether: what is meant here specifically refers to wholesomeness already experienced and attained in the past, lost through regression in between, and now, through stopping, brought forth once again — this is what is meant by "arising through a habituation-cause." The true, uncontaminated attainment arising at the four fruits, however, involves no cause of ever having been experienced in a former life and then lost through regression in between — how, then, could this possibly be classed together with dhyāna now brought forth again through cultivating stopping? If one speaks generally of the first grade of the true, uncontaminated understanding of mind serving as the basis for the second grade of uncontaminated mind, and so on in the same way up through the ninth grade — with reference to this sense of a habituation-cause, then the uncontaminated attainment arising at all four fruits could indeed be called an arising through a habituation-cause. But since what is clarified here does not take this sense of a habituation-cause as its reference, it is instead said that what arises at the four fruits is, in every case, not an arising from any habituation-cause wholesome root.

zh: 復次，行者過去修習事理諸禪三昧，雖未得證成就，而已經修習今世善根時熟，藉修止為緣，悉皆開發，此亦是習因善根發也。類等佛命「善來」，無漏即發，三明八解一時具足。料揀亦有漏亦無漏，乃至非有漏非無漏，類例可知。
en: Furthermore: a practitioner who, in past lives, cultivated phenomenal and principle dhyāna-samādhis without yet bringing them to completed realization, and who, in this present life, has that wholesome root come to ripeness, brought forth in full through cultivating stopping as its condition — this, too, is an arising of a wholesome root through a habituation-cause. This is comparable to the Buddha's own summons, "Welcome!," through which the uncontaminated is brought forth at once, the three insights and the eight liberations all complete together in that same instant. The distinguishing of what is both contaminated and uncontaminated together, and, further still, what is neither contaminated nor uncontaminated, may be understood by this same pattern.

zh: 釋禪波羅蜜次第法門卷第三之下
en: End of Fascicle Three, Lower Part, of the Shi Chan Boluomi Cidi Famen.

This closing analysis draws the sharpest possible line under everything the fascicle has been building toward: contaminated attainments can be traced to a habituation-cause resurfacing from some past life, and so, the treatise allows, can some uncontaminated ones — uncontaminated conduct-practice, cultivation that takes principle as its object, and approximate wisdom. Genuinely uncontaminated wisdom — the direct seeing of truth itself, as opposed to an approximation of it — is the exception, because "habituation-cause" here means something attained in a former life, lost through regression, and now brought forth again. The disagreement between the Sarvāstivādin and Dharmaguptaka interpretations over retrogressible once-returners, non-returners, and arhats who fall back to the first fruit and then realize the fruit again is a genuine scholastic dispute the treatise reports rather than resolves — a reminder that even within the Abhidharma tradition this question did not have a single settled answer. This closes the fifth and final part of distinguishing that dhyāna's arising is not fixed, the fourth of verifying wholesome capacity's four parts, and — since the source text itself defers verifying unwholesome capacity (明驗惡根性) to fascicle 4 — the whole of fascicle 3.

quiz.q: On why dhyāna arises, what does the first master hold, and how does the text judge it?
options: simply enter concentration and every dhyāna arises; teaching only stopping, like an old physician using only milk; the text disagrees — stopping is one, yet what arises differs
quiz.why: "One master says: 'One need only cultivate entry into concentration as described above, and every dhyāna will arise of itself' ... much like an old-fashioned physician who relies solely on milk as medicine. The present treatise does not follow this view." Past roots as cause is the second master's view.

quiz.q: The second master says past roots are the cause and present stopping the condition. What simile illustrates this?
options: an old physician using only milk
land holds many herbs and trees, but without the same single rain they could not grow in their different kinds
quiz.why: "The various dhyānas already experienced and habituated to in past lives serve as the wholesome-root cause; cultivating stopping in this present life serves as the condition ... It is like dry land: although it holds various kinds of medicinal herbs, trees, and thickets ... if they were not all equally moistened by the same single rain, how could their different kinds possibly grow?"

quiz.q: Why does the quantity of dhyāna that arises differ, according to the text?
options: past habituation partial or complete, thick or thin, and present diligence or laziness, skillful means with or without wisdom
quiz.why: "It is entirely because practitioners' past habituation-causes are unequal in their partiality or completeness, and differ in thickness or thinness, and also because of the difference, in this present life, between diligence and laziness, and between skillful means joined with wisdom and skillful means without it."

quiz.q: Using the contemplation of impurity, how are "exhausted" and "not exhausted" distinguished, and what can be done once exhausted?
options: only impurity without the flowing light is "not exhausted," both is "exhausted"; then stopping alone does not advance, and one must contemplate the bones in earnest to reach the eight liberations by present effort
once exhausted nothing more can be done
quiz.why: "If, now, within stopping, only the contemplation of impurity is brought forth, without yet attaining the flowing light of the white bones, this is called 'not exhausted'; if brought forth in full, this is called 'exhausted.' If what was habituated in the past has already spent its full force, then, even continuing to cultivate stopping, no further progress will be made." Further progress then comes from present diligent cultivation.

quiz.q: Which five kinds of practitioner capacity does the text say should be considered?
options: those prone to regression, who maintain, who abide, who progress, who penetrate
quiz.why: "Here, one should distinguish this by passing through five kinds of practitioner capacity: those prone to regression; those who merely maintain their ground; those who abide steadily; those who progress; and those who penetrate through."

quiz.q: Among the arisings of true wisdom, which does the text say is never said to have a habituation-cause?
options: the uncontaminated path of vision, such as the forbearance of suffering
quiz.why: "If uncontaminated attainment on the path of vision, such as the forbearance of suffering, arises, it is never, under any account, said to have a habituation-cause behind its arising. If uncontaminated attainment on the path of cultivation arises, the teaching on this point is not fixed." Approximate wisdom, cultivation of principle, and conduct-practice may have one.
